passage: Coach's note, district kabaddi trials. Uday (15) was not selected; his best friend Harsha was. I watched Uday read the list on the notice board. His shoulders dropped, and for a moment he stood very still. Then Harsha came running, and Uday grabbed him in a hug and shouted, 'Told you! Told you, man!' He meant it; I've coached them both for three years, and I know his fake smile. Later I found Uday alone on the bench, retying his shoes over and over. He said, 'I'm so happy for him. I'm just… sad too. Is that bad?' I told him both feelings are allowed. Next: I'll meet Uday this week about what to work on for next season, and keep him in the practice squad. — Coach Pereira

passage:
Friday, 9 p.m.
The state quiz team list came out. Gautam's on it. I'm not. We practised together every lunch break since July, and he beat me by two points in the final round.
When they read his name, I screamed louder than anyone. I wasn't pretending. He's worked so hard, and he looked so shocked and happy, going red like a tomato. I'm glad. Really, really glad.
And also I cried in the bathroom for ten minutes before Maths.
Both things happened. I keep thinking one of them must be the fake one, but I don't think either is.
Going to bake him a cake shaped like a trophy. A bad cake. He'll love it.
— Jaya

qa.a: Jaya decides to bake Gautam a trophy-shaped cake, showing the gladness is real even while the disappointment is still there. 🙂

qa.q: How might Gautam feel if Gautam knew about the ten minutes in the bathroom?
qa.a: Gautam might feel touched and a bit sad, and value Jaya's loud cheering even more, knowing what it cost.

passage: The list for the district volleyball team was pinned outside the staffroom of the high school in Sangamner. Mehak, fifteen, read it twice. Sonali Gaikwad. Not Mehak Shinde. Behind her, Sonali squeaked. Mehak spun round and hugged her so hard they both nearly fell. "You did it! Your serve, na? I told you!" She meant every word. They had practised on the dusty ground behind the temple every evening since June, and Sonali's serve had got better than hers. Sonali kept saying, "Sorry, sorry, you should've come too." "Stop. Go and tell your aai." Later, walking home alone past the sugarcane, Mehak let herself cry a little. She was happy for Sonali. She was sad for herself. Both felt completely true.

qa.a: She could tell someone she trusts at home that she's disappointed, and keep practising for next year, without taking back her joy for Sonali.

qa.q: How might Sonali feel about being chosen without Mehak?
qa.a: Sonali is thrilled but also guilty, which is why Sonali keeps apologising to Mehak.

grounding: A teen not picked for the team is truly glad for her best friend who was, and grieves a little too.

passage: The relay team for the regional swim meet in Vancouver was read out after practice. Four names. Clara's was the last. Kaito's wasn't there. Kaito, sixteen, was already clapping before he'd finished understanding, water still dripping from his hair. "Clara! Anchor leg!" She turned, stunned, and he high-fived her so hard it stung. He was glad, properly glad; she'd been coming to the pool at six every morning since September. On the bus home, though, he sat by the window and watched the rain on the glass. He'd been at the pool at six too. A quiet ache settled in his chest and stayed there, next to the happiness, neither one cancelling the other. He texted Clara: "Proud of you. Seriously." Then he put his head against the window.

qa.q: Which leg of the relay will Clara swim?
qa.a: The anchor leg.

qa.q: What was Kaito feeling on the bus home?
qa.a: A quiet ache at not being chosen, sitting alongside real happiness for Clara, with neither cancelling the other.

qa.q: What could help Kaito carry both feelings?
qa.a: He could let the disappointment be there without hiding it, maybe tell his coach or family he's sad, while still cheering for Clara at the meet.

qa.q: How might Clara feel reading Kaito's text?
qa.a: Clara would likely feel warmed and relieved that her friend is truly proud, not resentful.
